title: Esther (Greek)

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 1
summaryBullets: In the second year of the reign of Artaxerxes the Great, on the first day of Nisan, Mordecai son of Jair son of Shimei son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, had a dream. (1:2).
He was a Jew living in the city of Susa, a great man serving in the court of the king. (1:3).
He was one of the captives whom King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had taken captive from Jerusalem with King Jeconiah of Judea. And this was his dream: (1:4).
Noises and confusion, thunder and earthquake, tumult on the earth! (1:5).
Then two great dragons came forward, both ready to fight, and they roared terribly. (1:6).
At their roaring every nation prepared for war, to fight against a nation of righteous people. (1:7).
It was a day of darkness and gloom, of tribulation and distress, affliction and great tumult on the earth! (1:8).
And the whole righteous nation was troubled; they feared the evils that threatened them and were ready to perish. (1:9).
Then they cried out to God, and at their outcry, as though from a tiny spring, there came a great river with abundant water; (1:10).
light came, and the sun rose, and the lowly were exalted and devoured those held in honor. (1:11).
Mordecai saw in this dream what God had determined to do, and after he awoke he had it on his mind, seeking all day to understand it in every detail. (1:12).
crossRefs: Esther 2:5-6: The Hebrew introduces Mordecai son of Jair son of Shimei son of Kish, a Benjaminite carried off from Jerusalem with Jeconiah.
2 Kings 24:14-16: Jehoiachin, the officials, the warriors, and the craftsmen of Jerusalem are deported to Babylon.
1 Samuel 9:1-2: Kish the Benjaminite named as the father of Saul.
Daniel 8:15-17: Daniel seeks to understand a vision he has seen, and an interpreter is sent to explain it.
Joel 2:1-2: A day of darkness and gloom announced with trumpet and alarm.

translationNotes.original: Greek: Ἀρταξέρξης (Artaxerxes)
translationNotes.note: The Greek calls the king Artaxerxes at every point in the book. The Hebrew Esther calls the same king Ahasuerus. A reader comparing the two books meets one story under two royal names.

translationNotes.original: Greek: τῇ μιᾷ τοῦ Νισα (te mia tou Nisa)
translationNotes.note: Nisan is the first month of the Hebrew year, falling across March and April, the month of Passover. A date given as the first of Nisan stands at the head of the year.

translationNotes.original: Greek: μετὰ Ιεχονιου τοῦ βασιλέως τῆς Ιουδαίας (meta Iechoniou tou basileos tes Ioudaias)
translationNotes.note: Jeconiah is Jehoiachin, king of Judah, carried to Babylon with the officials and skilled men of Jerusalem in the deportation that came before the city itself fell.

translationNotes.original: Greek: δύο δράκοντες μεγάλοι (dyo drakontes megaloi)
translationNotes.note: The Greek drakon means a great serpent or sea creature, and the translators used it for the Hebrew tannin. It carries none of the winged, fire-breathing sense that the English word picked up later.

stories.keyTakeaway: On the first of Nisan in Artaxerxes' second year, Mordecai, a Jewish exile serving in the court at Susa, dreams of thunder, two roaring dragons, and the nations massed against a righteous people who cry to God. A tiny spring becomes a river, light rises, and the lowly are exalted.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 2
summaryBullets: Now Mordecai took his rest in the courtyard with Gabatha and Tharra, the two eunuchs of the king who kept watch in the courtyard. (2:1).
He overheard their conversation and inquired into their purposes and learned that they were preparing to lay hands on King Artaxerxes, and he informed the king concerning them. (2:2).
Then the king examined the two eunuchs, and after they had confessed it, they were led away. (2:3).
The king wrote these things down as a commemoration, and Mordecai wrote an account of them. (2:4).
And the king ordered Mordecai to serve in the court and rewarded him for these things. (2:5).
But Haman son of Hammedatha, a Bougean, who was in great honor with the king, determined to injure Mordecai and his people because of the two eunuchs of the king. (2:6).
crossRefs: Esther 2:21-23: The Hebrew names the two conspirators Bigthan and Teresh and has the matter written in the royal annals.
Ezra 4:15: A Persian king is asked to have the book of records of his predecessors searched.
Genesis 40:1-4: Pharaoh's chief cupbearer and chief baker, officers of the court, are put under guard after offending the king.
1 Samuel 15:8-9: Saul spares Agag king of the Amalekites and the best of the spoil.
Nehemiah 2:1-2: A Jew serving as cupbearer stands before the Persian king in the palace.

translationNotes.original: Greek: εὐνοῦχος (eunouchos)
translationNotes.note: A castrated officer of the royal household. Persian kings used them as bedchamber guards, keepers of the women, and cupbearers, since they could found no line of their own. The word also came to cover trusted court officers in general.

translationNotes.original: Greek: Γαβαθα καὶ Θαρρα (Gabatha kai Tharra)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew names the same two men Bigthan and Teresh. Greek copies of Esther spell Persian names loosely, so the same person can appear under two quite different forms.

translationNotes.original: Greek: Βουγαῖος (Bougaios)
translationNotes.note: Haman's description in the Greek. The Hebrew instead calls him an Agagite, tying him to Agag king of the Amalekites in 1 Samuel 15. Bougaios is not a translation of that word.

translationNotes.original: Greek: θεραπεύειν ἐν τῇ αὐλῇ (therapeuein en te aule)
translationNotes.note: A salaried post attending the king inside the palace enclosure, not a servant's job. The Hebrew describes the same standing as sitting in the king's gate, where royal business was transacted.

stories.keyTakeaway: Mordecai rests in the courtyard with Gabatha and Tharra, the eunuchs on watch, overhears their plan to lay hands on Artaxerxes, and reports them. They confess and are led away. The king records it and gives Mordecai a rewarded post at court. Haman the Bougean resolves to injure Mordecai and his people.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 3
summaryBullets: It was after this that the following things happened in the days of Artaxerxes, the same Artaxerxes who ruled over one hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia. (3:1).
In those days, when King Artaxerxes was enthroned in the city of Susa, (3:2).
in the third year of his reign, he gave a banquet for his Friends and other persons of various nations, the Persians and Median nobles, and the governors of the satrapies. (3:3).
After this, when he had displayed to them the riches of his kingdom and the splendor of his bountiful celebration during the course of one hundred eighty days, (3:4).
at the end of the wedding feast the king gave a drinking party for the people of various nations who lived in the city. This was held for six days in the courtyard of the royal palace, (3:5).

which was adorned with curtains of fine linen and cotton, held by cords of linen and purple fabric attached to gold and silver blocks on pillars of marble and other stones. Gold and silver couches were placed on a mosaic floor of emerald, mother-of-pearl, and marble. There were coverings of gauze, embroidered in various colors, with roses scattered around them. (3:6).
The cups were of gold and silver, and a miniature cup was displayed, made of ruby, worth thirty thousand talents. There was abundant sweet wine, such as the king himself drank. (3:7).
This drinking party was not in accordance with established custom, but the king wished to have it so, and he commanded his stewards to comply with his pleasure and with that of the guests. (3:8).
Meanwhile, Queen Vashti gave a drinking party for the women in the palace where King Artaxerxes was. (3:9).
On the seventh day, when the king was in good humor, he told Haman, Bazan, Tharra, Boraze, Zatholtha, Abataza, and Tharaba, the seven eunuchs who served King Artaxerxes, (3:10).

to escort the queen to him in order to proclaim her as queen and to place the diadem on her head and to have her display her beauty to all the governors and the people of various nations, for she was indeed a beautiful woman. (3:11).
But Queen Vashti refused to obey him and would not come with the eunuchs. This offended the king, and he became furious. (3:12).
He said to his Friends, “This is how Vashti has answered me. Give, therefore, your ruling and judgment on this matter.” (3:13).
Arkesaeus, Sarsathaeus, and Malesear, the governors of the Persians and Medes who were closest to the king, who sat beside him in the chief seats, came to him (3:14).
and told him what, according to the law, was to be done to Queen Vashti for not obeying the order that the king had sent her by the eunuchs. (3:15).
Then Muchaeus said to the king and to the officials, “Queen Vashti has not wronged the king alone, but also all the king’s officials and governors, (3:16).
(for he had reported to them the words of the queen and how she had contradicted the king). So, just as she contradicted King Artaxerxes, (3:17).
so now the other noble wives of the rulers of the Persians and the Medes, when they hear what she said to the king, will dare in the same way to dishonor their husbands. (3:18).

If, therefore, it pleases the king, let him issue a royal decree, and let it be written among the laws of the Medes and the Persians, and let it not be altered, that the queen may come in to him no more; and let the king give her royal rank to a woman better than she. (3:19).
Let whatever law the king enacts be proclaimed throughout his kingdom, and then all the women will give honor to their husbands, from the poor to the rich.” (3:20).
This speech pleased the king and the officials, and the king did as Muchaeus had said. (3:21).
The king sent the decree into all his kingdom, province by province, each in its own language, so that every man might be respected in his own household. (3:22).
crossRefs: Esther 1:1-22: The Hebrew account of the same feast, the queen's refusal, and the decree that followed.
Daniel 6:8: A decree written under the law of the Medes and Persians cannot be revoked.
Ezra 1:1-2: A Persian king sends a proclamation in writing throughout his whole kingdom.
Nehemiah 1:1: Susa named as the fortified royal residence where the king's business is done.
Daniel 5:1-4: A king holds a great feast for a thousand of his lords and drinks wine before them.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֵהֹדּוּ וְעַד־כּוּשׁ (me-Hoddu ve-ad Kush) - Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰνδικῆς ἕως τῆς Αἰθιοπίας (apo tes Indikes heos tes Aithiopias)
translationNotes.note: Hoddu is the Indus country at the eastern edge of Persian rule; Kush is Nubia, on the Nile south of Egypt, not the modern nation called Ethiopia. The pair names the two ends of the empire.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנִים (achashdarpenim) - Greek: σατράπαι (satrapai)
translationNotes.note: A satrap governed a large administrative region for the Persian king, collecting tribute and raising troops. The word comes from Old Persian for protector of the realm. The hundred twenty-seven provinces were smaller districts inside those regions.

translationNotes.original: Greek: οἱ φίλοι (hoi philoi)
translationNotes.note: A formal rank at court, not personal friendship. Friends of the king held office, drew royal gifts, and were graded by precedence. Being seated first among the Friends was a promotion, not a compliment.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַשְׁתִּי (Vashti) - Greek: Αστιν (Astin)
translationNotes.note: The Greek text spells the queen's name Astin throughout. English versions of the Greek print the familiar Hebrew form Vashti, so the difference does not show on the page.

stories.keyTakeaway: Artaxerxes, ruling one hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia, feasts his nobles and satraps at Susa for one hundred eighty days, then holds a six-day drinking party while Queen Vashti feasts the women. She refuses to appear in the diadem, and on Muchaeus's advice the king strips her rank by unalterable law.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 4
summaryBullets: After these things, the king’s anger abated, and he no longer remembered Vashti or remembered what he had said and how he had condemned her. (4:1).
Then the king’s servants said, “Let beautiful and virtuous young women be sought out for the king. (4:2).

The king shall appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, and they shall select beautiful young virgins to be brought to the harem in the city of Susa. Let them be entrusted to the king’s eunuch who is in charge of the women, and let ointments and whatever else they need be given them. (4:3).
And the woman who pleases the king shall be queen instead of Vashti.” This pleased the king, and he did so. (4:4).
Now there was a Jew in the city of Susa whose name was Mordecai son of Jair son of Shimei son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin; (4:5).
he had been taken captive from Jerusalem among those whom King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had captured. (4:6).

And he had a foster child, the daughter of his father’s brother, Aminadab, and her name was Esther. When her parents died, he brought her up as a wife for himself. The young woman was beautiful in appearance. (4:7).
So when the decree of the king was proclaimed and many young women were gathered in the city of Susa in custody of Gai, Esther also was brought to Gai, who had custody of the women. (4:8).

The young woman pleased him and won his favor, and he quickly provided her with ointments and her portion of food, as well as seven young women chosen from the palace; he treated her and her maids with special favor in the harem. (4:9).
Now Esther had not disclosed her people or country, for Mordecai had commanded her not to make it known. (4:10).
And every day Mordecai walked in the courtyard of the harem, to see what would happen to Esther. (4:11).

Now the period after which a young woman was to go to the king was twelve months. During this time the days of cosmetic treatment are completed: six months while they are anointing themselves with oil of myrrh and six months with spices and ointments for women. (4:12).
Then she goes in to the king; she is handed to the person appointed and goes with him from the harem to the king’s palace. (4:13).

In the evening she enters, and in the morning she departs to the second harem, where Gai the king’s eunuch is in charge of the women, and she does not go in to the king again unless she is summoned by name. (4:14).

When the time was fulfilled for Esther daughter of Aminadab, the brother of Mordecai’s father, to go in to the king, she neglected none of the things that the eunuch in charge of the women had commanded. For Esther found favor in the eyes of all who saw her. (4:15).
So Esther went in to King Artaxerxes in the twelfth month, which is Adar, in the seventh year of his reign. (4:16).
And the king loved Esther passionately, and she found favor beyond all the other virgins, and he put on her the queen’s diadem. (4:17).

Then the king gave a drinking party lasting seven days for all his Friends and the officers of state, to celebrate the marriage of Esther, and he proclaimed a release for those under his rule. (4:18).
Meanwhile Mordecai was serving in the court. (4:19).

Esther had not disclosed her country, for so Mordecai had commanded her: to fear God and to keep his commandments, just as she had done when she was with him. So Esther did not change her manner of life. (4:20).
Now two of the king’s eunuchs, who were chief of the bodyguard, were grieved that Mordecai had been advanced, and they sought to kill King Artaxerxes. (4:21).
The matter became known to Mordecai, and he told Esther, and she disclosed to the king what the conspiracy was. (4:22).
He investigated the two eunuchs and hanged them. Then the king ordered a record to be made as a memorial in the royal library, commending the goodwill of Mordecai. (4:23).
crossRefs: Esther 2:1-23: The Hebrew account, which calls the eunuch Hegai, names Esther's father Abihail, and says Mordecai took her as his own daughter.
Genesis 41:39-45: Pharaoh sets a Hebrew over Egypt, renames him, and gives him a wife from the priestly household.
Daniel 1:3-6: Young men without blemish and skilled in learning are selected and trained for service in a foreign king's palace.
1 Kings 1:1-4: Officers search the whole territory for a beautiful young woman to bring to the king.
Esther 2:16: The Hebrew dates Esther's coming to the king in Tebeth, the tenth month, of his seventh year.

translationNotes.term: Gai, who had custody of the women
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֵגַי (Hegai) - Greek: Γαι (Gai)
translationNotes.note: The keeper of the women ran the separate quarters where the king's wives and candidates lived, controlled who entered, and issued their food, cosmetics, and attendants. The Hebrew spells his name Hegai.

translationNotes.term: He brought her up as a wife for himself
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְבַת (le-vat, as a daughter) - Greek: εἰς γυναῖκα (eis gynaika, as a wife)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew says Mordecai took the orphaned Esther as a daughter. The Greek reads that he raised her for himself as a wife. The Greek also names her father Aminadab where the Hebrew has Abihail.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֶׁמֶן הַמֹּר (shemen ha-mor) - Greek: σμύρνινον ἔλαιον (smyrninon elaion)
translationNotes.note: Myrrh is a fragrant resin tapped from a desert shrub and steeped in oil. The twelve months of treatment, six with myrrh oil and six with spices, were a required regimen of the harem, not a personal luxury.

translationNotes.term: In the twelfth month, which is Adar
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲדָר (Adar) - Greek: Αδαρ (Adar)
translationNotes.note: Adar is the last month of the Hebrew year, falling across February and March. Here the Greek and Hebrew differ on the date: the Greek brings Esther to the king in Adar, the Hebrew in Tebeth, the tenth month.

stories.keyTakeaway: With the king's anger spent, virgins are gathered to Susa under the eunuch Gai. Esther, Mordecai's foster child, wins favor there but hides her people. After a year of ointments she goes in to Artaxerxes, who loves her, sets the queen's diadem on her, and feasts seven days. Mordecai then exposes two eunuchs plotting the king's death.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 5
summaryBullets: After these events King Artaxerxes honored Haman son of Hammedatha, a Bougean, and exalted him, and would seat him first among all the king’s Friends. (5:1).
So all who were at court used to do obeisance to Haman, for so the king had commanded to be done. Mordecai, however, did not do obeisance. (5:2).
Then the king’s courtiers said to Mordecai, “Mordecai, why do you disobey the king’s command?” (5:3).
Day after day they spoke to him, but he would not listen to them. Then they informed Haman that Mordecai was resisting the king’s command. Mordecai had told them that he was a Jew. (5:4).
So when Haman learned that Mordecai was not doing obeisance to him, he became furiously angry (5:5).
and resolved to destroy all the Jews under Artaxerxes’s rule. (5:6).

In the twelfth year of the reign of Artaxerxes, Haman came to a decision and cast lots, taking the days and the months one by one, to fix on one day to destroy the whole people of Mordecai. The lot fell on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar. (5:7).

Then Haman said to King Artaxerxes, “There is a certain nation scattered among the other nations in all your kingdom; their laws are different from those of every other nation, and they do not keep the laws of the king. It is not expedient for the king to tolerate them. (5:8).
If it pleases the king, let him decree that they are to be destroyed, and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver into the king’s treasury.” (5:9).
So the king took off his signet ring and gave it to Haman to seal the decree that was to be written against the Jews. (5:10).
The king told Haman, “Keep the money, and do whatever you want with that nation.” (5:11).

So on the thirteenth day of the first month the king’s secretaries were summoned, and in accordance with Haman’s instructions they wrote in the name of King Artaxerxes to the magistrates and the governors in every province from India to Ethiopia, one hundred twenty-seven provinces in all, and to the governors of the nations, each in his own language. (5:12).
Instructions were sent by couriers throughout all the empire of Artaxerxes to destroy the Jewish people in a single day of the twelfth month, which is Adar, and to plunder their goods. ——— (5:13).
crossRefs: Esther 3:1-13: The Hebrew account, which calls Haman an Agagite and names the lot pur.
Daniel 3:8-12: Men are accused before a king for refusing to bow down to what he has set up.
Ezra 4:12-16: A letter to a Persian king charging a people with laws and conduct hostile to the crown.
Genesis 41:42: Pharaoh takes his signet ring from his own hand and puts it on Joseph.
Proverbs 16:33: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.

translationNotes.original: Greek: προσκυνέω (proskyneo)
translationNotes.note: Full prostration before a superior, face to the ground. Persian court protocol required it of everyone admitted to the king's presence and of those he raised to high rank. Greeks found the practice foreign and remarked on it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פּוּר (pur), glossed in Esther 3:7 as גּוֹרָל (goral, lot) - Greek: κλῆρος (kleros)
translationNotes.note: Marked objects were thrown to settle a question without human choice. The Hebrew keeps the Persian loanword pur and explains it; the Greek simply uses its ordinary word for a lot, so the loanword does not appear here.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּכָּר (kikkar) - Greek: τάλαντον (talanton)
translationNotes.note: A talent is a unit of weight, not a skill or ability. One ran about seventy-five pounds. Ten thousand talents of silver is on the order of three hundred tons, a sum in the range of a year's tribute from the whole empire.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: טַבַּעַת (tabbaat) - Greek: δακτύλιος (daktylios)
translationNotes.note: The ring carried the king's seal. Pressed into clay or wax on a document, it made the order the king's own act. Handing the ring over transferred the power to issue orders in the king's name.

stories.keyTakeaway: Artaxerxes exalts Haman the Bougean above all his Friends. Every courtier bows but Mordecai, who tells them he is a Jew. Enraged, Haman casts lots and the day falls on the fourteenth of Adar. He offers ten thousand talents to destroy the Jews; the king hands him the signet ring, and couriers carry the order to every province.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 6
summaryBullets: This is a copy of the letter: “The Great King, Artaxerxes, writes the following to the governors of the hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia and to the officials under them: (6:1).

“Having become ruler of many nations and master of the whole world (not elated with presumption of authority but always acting reasonably and with kindness), I have determined to settle the lives of my subjects in lasting tranquility and, in order to make my kingdom peaceable and open to travel throughout all its extent, to restore the peace desired by all people. (6:2).

“When I asked my counselors how this might be accomplished, Haman—who excels among us in sound judgment and is distinguished for his unchanging goodwill and steadfast fidelity and has attained the second place of honor in the kingdom— (6:3).

pointed out to us that among all the nations in the world there is scattered a certain hostile people who have laws contrary to those of every nation and continually disregard the ordinances of kings, so that the unifying of the kingdom that we honorably intend cannot be brought about. (6:4).

We understand that this people, and it alone, stands constantly in opposition to all humanity, perversely following a strange manner of life and laws, and is ill-disposed to our interests, doing all the harm they can so that our kingdom may not attain stability. (6:5).

“Therefore we have decreed that those indicated to you in the letters written by Haman, who is in charge of affairs and is our second father, shall all—wives and children included—be utterly destroyed by the swords of their enemies, without pity or restraint, on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, of this present year, (6:6).
so that those who have long been hostile and remain so may in a single day go down in violence to Hades and leave our interests secure and untroubled hereafter.” (6:7).
crossRefs: Esther 3:12-15: The Hebrew records the same letters sent by couriers, dating the day the thirteenth of Adar.
Ezra 4:17-22: A Persian king's written reply, addressed to named officials, ordering work to stop at once.
Daniel 3:4-6: A herald proclaims to every people and language what they must do on pain of death.
Genesis 45:8: Joseph says God has made him a father to Pharaoh and ruler over all Egypt.
Numbers 16:31-33: Men go down alive into Sheol, the realm of the dead the Greek calls Hades.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἀντίγραφον τῆς ἐπιστολῆς (antigraphon tes epistoles)
translationNotes.note: A royal order took effect through certified copies sent out to each province while the original stayed in the chancery. Quoting the copy in full is standard practice for official correspondence.

translationNotes.original: Greek: δεύτερος πατὴρ ἡμῶν (deuteros pater hemon)
translationNotes.note: Father was a title of honor at royal courts, given to the highest minister rather than to a parent. It ranks Haman as first among the king's men, with the second place of honor in the kingdom.

translationNotes.original: Greek: πάσης ἐπικρατήσας οἰκουμένης (pases epikratesas oikoumenes)
translationNotes.note: The oikoumene is the inhabited world as the writer knows it, the settled lands under civilized rule. Persian royal titles claimed the whole of it, king of lands and king of kings.

translationNotes.term: Go down in violence to Hades
translationNotes.original: Greek: εἰς τὸν ᾅδην (eis ton haden)
translationNotes.note: Hades is the Greek name for the realm of the dead, the word the translators used for the Hebrew Sheol. In a royal decree it is a blunt way of saying the whole people is to be killed in one day.

stories.keyTakeaway: The letter is quoted in full. Artaxerxes writes to the governors of his one hundred twenty-seven provinces that he rules with restraint and wants lasting peace, and that Haman, second in the kingdom, has shown him one scattered people whose laws differ from every nation's. He orders them all destroyed by the sword on the fourteenth of Adar.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 7
summaryBullets: Copies of the letter were posted in every province, and all the nations were ordered to be ready for that day. (7:14).
The matter was expedited also in Susa. And while the king and Haman drank together, the city was thrown into confusion. (7:15).
crossRefs: Esther 3:15: The Hebrew ends the same scene with the king and Haman sitting down to drink while the city of Susa is thrown into confusion.
Ezra 6:11: A Persian decree is published with the penalty for anyone who alters it.
Daniel 6:9-10: A written edict is issued and the man it targets learns that the document has been signed.
Amos 8:11-13: A land thrown into distress, its people staggering from one end to the other.
Habakkuk 2:15-16: Woe to the one who makes his neighbors drink and looks on their ruin.

translationNotes.original: Greek: τὰ ἀντίγραφα ἐξετίθετο (ta antigrapha exetitheto)
translationNotes.note: The verb means to set out in public view. A decree became law in a province when its written copy was displayed where people gathered, which is how the whole empire learned of an order on the same schedule.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוּשַׁן הַבִּירָה (Shushan ha-birah) - Greek: Σοῦσα (Sousa)
translationNotes.note: Susa had two parts, the walled citadel holding the palace and the administration, and the town below it. The Hebrew marks the difference by naming Susa the citadel; the English here renders both simply as Susa.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐκωθωνίζοντο (ekothonizonto)
translationNotes.note: The verb is built on kothon, a broad drinking cup, and means to drink deep or carouse. The English is milder than the Greek, which has the two men settling in over their cups while the city outside panics.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἑτοίμους εἶναι (hetoimous einai)
translationNotes.note: The decree set a date rather than taking effect at once. Written in the first month for a day in the twelfth, it gave every province eleven months' notice, and the order stands published that whole time.

stories.keyTakeaway: Copies of the letter are posted in every province, and all the nations are ordered to be ready for that day. The business is pressed forward in Susa as well. The king and Haman sit down to drink together, and the city is thrown into confusion.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 8
summaryBullets: When Mordecai learned of all that had been done, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and sprinkled himself with ashes; then he rushed through the street of the city, shouting loudly: “An innocent nation is being destroyed!” (8:1).
He got as far as the king’s gate, and there he stopped, because no one was allowed to enter the courtyard clothed in sackcloth and ashes. (8:2).
And in every province where the letter had been posted there was crying, lamentation, and great mourning among the Jews, and they put on sackcloth and ashes. (8:3).

When the queen’s maids and eunuchs came and told her, she was deeply troubled by what she heard had happened and sent instructions to clothe Mordecai and to remove his sackcloth, but he would not consent. (8:4).
Then Esther summoned Hachratheus, the eunuch who attended her, and dispatched him to get accurate information for her from Mordecai. (8:5).
So Mordecai told him what had happened and about the promise that Haman had promised the king: ten thousand talents for the royal treasury to bring about the destruction of the Jews. (8:7).

He also gave him a copy of what had been posted in Susa for their destruction, to show to Esther, and he told him to charge her to go in to the king and plead for his favor in behalf of the people. “Remember,” he said, “the days when you were an ordinary person, being brought up under my care, for Haman, who is second to the king, has spoken against us and demands our death. Call upon the Lord; then speak to the king in our behalf and save us from death.” (8:8).
Hachratheus went in and told her all these things. (8:9).
And Esther said to him, “Go to Mordecai and say: (8:10).

All nations of the realm know that if any man or woman goes to the king inside the inner court without being called, there is no escape for that person. Only the one to whom the king stretches out the golden scepter is safe—and it is now thirty days since I myself was called to go to the king.” (8:11).
So Hachratheus delivered Esther’s entire message to Mordecai, (8:12).
and then Mordecai said to Hachratheus, “Go and say to her: Esther, do not say to yourself that you alone among all the Jews in the realm will escape alive. (8:13).

For if you take no heed at such a time as this, help and protection will come to the Jews from another quarter, but you and your father’s family will perish. And who knows whether it was not for such a time as this that you were made queen?” (8:14).
Then Esther gave the messenger this answer to take back to Mordecai: (8:15).

“Go and gather the Jews who are in Susa and fast on my behalf; for three days and nights do not eat or drink, and my maids and I will also go without food. After that I will go to the king, contrary to the law, even if I must die.” (8:16).
So Mordecai went away and did what Esther had told him to do. (8:17).
crossRefs: Esther 4:1-17: The Hebrew account, which calls the eunuch Hathach and has Esther ask that the Jews of Susa fast for her.
Genesis 37:34: Jacob tears his clothes, puts sackcloth on his loins, and mourns many days.
Jonah 3:5-9: A whole city fasts in sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least.
Daniel 2:17-18: Daniel tells his companions of the decree and asks them to seek mercy from God.
Nehemiah 2:1-3: A Jew in the Persian court is afraid when the king notices the sadness on his face.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק וָאֵפֶר (saq va-efer) - Greek: σάκκος καὶ σποδός (sakkos kai spodos)
translationNotes.note: Coarse dark cloth of goat hair worn against the skin, with hearth ash poured over the head. It was the public dress of grief and urgent petition. Court rules barred it from the palace, which is why Mordecai can go no further than the gate.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֲתָךְ (Hathach) - Greek: Αχραθαῖος (Achrathaios)
translationNotes.note: The eunuch assigned to attend the queen. Because women of the household did not move freely through the palace, an attendant like this carried messages in and out, which is why every exchange here passes through him.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁרְבִיט הַזָּהָב (sharvit ha-zahav) - Greek: χρυσῆ ῥάβδος (chryse rhabdos)
translationNotes.note: A gold rod held by the seated king. Anyone entering the inner court unsummoned was killed unless he extended it toward them. The gesture was a pardon for the intrusion, granted or withheld on the spot.

translationNotes.term: Three days and nights, do not eat or drink
translationNotes.original: Greek: νηστεύσατε ἐπ᾽ ἐμοί (nesteusate ep' emoi)
translationNotes.note: A total fast, food and water alike, kept through the nights as well as the days. Ordinary fasts ran from dawn to dusk with drinking allowed, so the wording marks this one as far more severe.

stories.keyTakeaway: Mordecai puts on sackcloth and ashes and cries through Susa that an innocent nation is being destroyed. Hearing by the eunuch Hachratheus, Esther answers that anyone entering the king uncalled dies unless he extends the golden scepter. Mordecai warns she will not escape alone, so she orders a three-day fast and resolves to go.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 9
summaryBullets: Then Mordecai prayed to the Lord, calling to remembrance all the works of the Lord. (9:8).
He said, “O Lord, Lord, King of all powers, for the universe is in your power and there is no one who can oppose you when it is your will to save Israel, (9:9).
for you have made heaven and earth and every wonderful thing under heaven. (9:10).
You are Lord of all, and there is no one who can resist you, the Lord. (9:11).
You know all things; you know, O Lord, that it was not in insolence or pride or for any love of glory that I did this and refused to bow down to this proud Haman, (9:12).
for I would have been willing to kiss the soles of his feet to save Israel! (9:13).
But I did this so that I might not set human glory above the glory of God, and I will not bow down to anyone but you, who are my Lord, and I will not do these things in pride. (9:14).

And now, O Lord God and King, God of Abraham, spare your people, for the eyes of our foes are upon us to annihilate us, and they desire to destroy the inheritance that has been yours from the beginning. (9:15).
Do not neglect your portion, which you redeemed for yourself out of the land of Egypt. (9:16).
Hear my prayer and have mercy upon your inheritance; turn our mourning into feasting that we may live and sing praise to your name, O Lord; do not destroy the lips of those who praise you.” (9:17).
And all Israel cried out with all their might, for their death was before their eyes. (9:18).
crossRefs: Nehemiah 9:6: A prayer confessing the Lord as maker of heaven, earth, and all their host.
Deuteronomy 9:26-29: Moses prays that God not destroy the people He redeemed and brought out of Egypt as His own portion.
Exodus 20:3-5: The command not to bow down or serve anything besides God.
1 Chronicles 29:11-12: A prayer ascribing all greatness, power, and dominion in heaven and earth to God.
Daniel 9:4-19: A prayer offered for a people under sentence, appealing to God's own name and inheritance.

translationNotes.term: O Lord, Lord, King of all powers
translationNotes.original: Greek: κύριε κύριε βασιλεῦ πάντων κρατῶν (kyrie kyrie basileu panton kraton)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew book of Esther never names God at any point. The Greek does, and does it first here, addressing Him directly in the language of royal titles.

translationNotes.term: Kiss the soles of his feet
translationNotes.original: Greek: φιλῆσαι τὰ ἴχνη τῶν ποδῶν αὐτοῦ (philesai ta ichne ton podon autou)
translationNotes.note: The most abject form of the prostration required at court. Saying he would do even this makes the point that his refusal to bow was not about the indignity of the gesture.

translationNotes.original: Greek: κληρονομία (kleronomia), μερίς (meris), κλῆρος (kleros)
translationNotes.note: Three words for an allotted share, the vocabulary of dividing land by lot. The last of them, kleros, is the same word used for the lot Haman cast, a link the English cannot show.

translationNotes.term: Redeemed for yourself out of Egypt
translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐλυτρώσω (elytroso)
translationNotes.note: The verb means to buy back by paying a price, the ordinary word for ransoming a captive or a slave. It is the standard Greek rendering for what God did at the exodus.

stories.keyTakeaway: Mordecai prays, calling to remembrance the works of the Lord: God is King of all powers, maker of heaven and earth, and no one can resist Him. He says he refused to bow to Haman from no pride or love of glory, and would kiss the man's feet to save Israel. He asks God to spare His people and turn their mourning into feasting, and all Israel cries out.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 10
summaryBullets: Then Queen Esther, seized with mortal anguish, fled to the Lord. (10:1).

She took off the garments of her honor and put on the garments of distress and mourning, and instead of costly perfumes she covered her head with ashes and dung, and she utterly humbled her body; every part that she loved to adorn she covered with her tangled hair. (10:2).
She prayed to the Lord God of Israel and said: “O my Lord, you alone are our king; help me, who am alone and have no helper but you, (10:3).
for my danger is in my hand. (10:4).

Ever since I was born I have heard in the tribe of my family that you, O Lord, took Israel out of all the nations and our ancestors from among all their forebears for an everlasting inheritance and that you did for them all that you said. (10:5).
And now we have sinned before you, and you have delivered us into the hands of our enemies (10:6).
because we glorified their gods. You are righteous, O Lord! (10:7).
And now they are not satisfied that we are in bitter slavery, but they have set their hands on the hands of their idols (10:8).
to abolish what your mouth has ordained and to destroy your inheritance, to stop the mouths of those who praise you and to quench your altar and the glory of your house, (10:9).
to open the mouths of the nations for the praise of vain idols and to magnify forever a mortal king. (10:10).
“O Lord, do not surrender your scepter to what has no being, and do not let them laugh at our downfall, but turn their plan against them and make an example of him who began this against us. (10:11).
Remember, O Lord; make yourself known in this time of our affliction and give me courage, O King of the gods and Master of all dominion! (10:12).
Put eloquent speech in my mouth before the lion and turn his heart to hate the man who is fighting against us, so that there may be an end of him and those who agree with him. (10:13).
Save us by your hand, and help me, who am alone and have no helper but you, O Lord. You have knowledge of all things, (10:14).
and you know that I hate the splendor of the wicked and abhor the bed of the uncircumcised and of any alien. (10:15).

You know my necessity, that I abhor the sign of my proud position, which is upon my head on days when I appear in public. I abhor it like a filthy rag, and I do not wear it on the days when I am at leisure. (10:16).
And your servant has not eaten at Haman's table, and I have not honored the king's feast or drunk the wine of libations. (10:17).
Your servant has had no joy since the day that I was brought here until now, except in you, O Lord God of Abraham. (10:18).
O God, whose might is over all, hear the voice of the despairing, and save us from the hands of evildoers. And save me from my fear!” (10:19).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 7:6-8: The Lord chose Israel out of all the peoples on the earth to be His own.
Daniel 9:5-11: A confession that the people sinned and were handed over to the curse written in the law.
Psalm 115:4-8: Idols of silver and gold, the work of human hands, that have mouths and cannot speak.
Exodus 34:15-16: A warning against eating from the sacrifices offered to the gods of other peoples.
Nehemiah 1:5-11: A prayer for mercy and for favor before a Persian king, made before any word is spoken to him.

translationNotes.original: Greek: σποδοῦ καὶ κοπριῶν (spodou kai koprion)
translationNotes.note: Hearth ash and refuse from the dung heap, heaped on the head. Mourners commonly used ash; adding koprion, the sweepings of the yard, takes the self-abasement to the lowest point the custom allowed.

translationNotes.term: The sign of my proud position
translationNotes.original: Greek: τὸ σημεῖον τῆς ὑπερηφανίας μου (to semeion tes hyperephanias mou)
translationNotes.note: The royal diadem, a band worn around the head, which she must wear on the days she appears in public. The Greek then likens it to a menstrual rag, a comparison English versions soften to a filthy rag.

translationNotes.original: Greek: οἶνον σπονδῶν (oinon spondon)
translationNotes.note: A libation is wine poured out to a god before the drinking begins. Wine served at a royal table had normally been offered that way first, so refusing it meant refusing the whole rite, not the drink.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐνώπιον τοῦ λέοντος (enopion tou leontos)
translationNotes.note: The lion is the king. Lions stood for royal power across the ancient Near East, carved along the processional ways of Babylon and glazed onto the palace walls at Susa itself.

stories.keyTakeaway: Esther strips off her royal dress for mourning, covers her head with ashes and dung, and prays to the God of Israel. She recounts His choice of Israel, confesses their sin, and says their enemies mean to silence His praise and magnify a mortal king. She begs for eloquent speech before the lion, and declares she abhors the diadem and Haman's table.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 11
summaryBullets: On the third day, when she ended her prayer, she took off the garments she had worn in her supplication and put on her splendid apparel. (11:1).
Then, in the full splendor of her adornment, she called upon the God who watches over all and saves, and she took two maids with her. (11:2).
She leaned on one of them, as a woman of delicate breeding, (11:3).
while the other followed behind her, carrying her train. (11:4).
She was radiant in the full flower of her beauty, and her face was cheerful, as though she were beloved, but her heart was gripped with fear. (11:5).

When she had gone through all the doors, she stood before the king. He was seated on his royal throne, clothed in the full splendor of his majesty, all covered with gold and precious stones, and he was terrifying to see. (11:6).
Lifting his face, blazing with glory, he looked at her in fierce anger. The queen faltered, turned pale and faint, and sank down on the head of the maid who went before her. (11:7).
Then God changed the spirit of the king to gentleness, and in alarm he sprang from his throne and took her in his arms until she recovered, comforting her with soothing words. (11:8).
He said to her, “What is it, Esther? I am your brother. Take courage; (11:9).
you shall not die, for our order concerns only our subjects. Come near.” (11:10).
Then he raised the golden scepter and laid it upon her neck, (11:11).
and he embraced her and said, “Speak to me.” (11:12).
She said to him, “I saw you, my lord, like an angel of God, and my heart was shaken with fear at your glory. (11:13).
For you are wonderful, my lord, and your face is full of grace.” (11:14).
And while she was speaking, she fainted and fell. (11:15).
Then the king was alarmed, and all his servants tried to comfort her. (11:16).
crossRefs: Esther 5:1-2: The Hebrew tells the same approach in two verses, with the king holding out the golden scepter and Esther touching its tip.
2 Samuel 14:17: A petitioner tells the king he is like an angel of God in discerning good and evil.
Proverbs 21:1: The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD, turned wherever He wills.
Ezra 7:27-28: Thanks that God put a thing in the king's heart and granted favor before the king and his counselors.
Daniel 10:8-10: A man's strength drains away at a terrifying sight and he falls, until a hand raises him.

translationNotes.term: When she had gone through all the doors
translationNotes.original: Greek: εἰσελθοῦσα πάσας τὰς θύρας (eiselthousa pasas tas thyras)
translationNotes.note: The Persian throne room sat behind a series of gated courts, each with its own guard. Passing them all is the point: by the last door she is past every place where she could have been turned back.

translationNotes.term: As a woman of delicate breeding
translationNotes.original: Greek: ὡς τρυφερευομένη (hos trypheruomene)
translationNotes.note: Leaning on one maid while another carries the train is court display, not weakness. A great lady of the household did not walk unsupported in public, and the attendants are part of the show of rank.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐγὼ ὁ ἀδελφός σου (ego ho adelphos sou)
translationNotes.note: Brother and sister served as terms of address between a king and his consort in the Near East, marking her as of his own household. It is reassurance about her standing, not a statement about blood.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ὡς ἄγγελον θεοῦ (hos angelon theou)
translationNotes.note: A set formula for addressing a king, used the same way by petitioners in 2 Samuel 14 and 19. It credits him with the discernment and dread of a heavenly messenger, and it is the expected speech of the court.

stories.keyTakeaway: On the third day Esther ends her prayer, dresses in splendor, and goes in with two maids, radiant to look at and gripped by fear. The king, blazing on his throne, looks at her in anger and she faints. God turns his spirit to gentleness; he takes her in his arms, tells her she will not die, and lays the golden scepter on her neck.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 12
summaryBullets: The king said to her, “What do you wish, Esther? What is your request? It shall be given you, even to half of my kingdom.” (12:3).
And Esther said, “Today is a special day for me. If it pleases the king, let him and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare today.” (12:4).
Then the king said, “Bring Haman quickly, so that we may do as Esther has said.” So the two of them came to the banquet that Esther had spoken of. (12:5).
While they were drinking wine, the king said to Esther, “What is it, Queen Esther? Whatever your request, it shall be granted.” (12:6).
She said, “My petition and my request are these: (12:7).
if I have found favor with the king, let the king and Haman come again tomorrow to the banquet that I shall prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as I have done today.” (12:8).
So Haman went out from the king in high spirits and rejoicing, but when he saw Mordecai the Jew in the courtyard, he was filled with rage. (12:9).
Nevertheless, he went home and summoned his friends and his wife Zosara. (12:10).
And he told them about his riches and the honor the king had given him, and how the king had advanced him to first place and the leadership of the kingdom. (12:11).
And Haman said, “The queen did not invite anyone to the banquet with the king except me, and I am invited again tomorrow. (12:12).
But these things give me no pleasure as long as I see Mordecai the Jew in the courtyard.” (12:13).

His wife Zosara and his friends said to him, “Let a pole fifty cubits high be made for you, and in the morning speak to the king and have Mordecai hanged on it. Then go with the king to the banquet and enjoy yourself.” The advice pleased Haman, and the pole was prepared. (12:14).
crossRefs: Esther 5:3-14: The Hebrew account, which names Haman's wife Zeresh and the timber fifty cubits high.
Mark 6:22-23: A king swears to a young woman that he will give her whatever she asks, up to half his kingdom.
Ezra 6:11: A Persian decree that a beam be pulled from the offender's house and he be impaled upon it.
1 Kings 21:4-7: A king turns sullen over the one thing he cannot have, and his wife tells him how to get it.
Nehemiah 2:4-6: A Persian king asks his servant what he requests, and grants it with a set time.

translationNotes.term: Even to half of my kingdom
translationNotes.original: Greek: ἕως τοῦ ἡμίσους τῆς βασιλείας μου (heos tou hemisous tes basileias mou)
translationNotes.note: A court formula of open-handedness, not a literal offer of territory. Herod uses the same words in Mark 6:23. It signals that the request will be granted, whatever it turns out to be.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐν τῷ πότῳ (en to poto)
translationNotes.note: The potos is the drinking session that followed the meal, a distinct event with its own etiquette. Petitions were raised there rather than at table, so the king's question comes at the expected moment.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵץ (ets) - Greek: ξύλον (xylon)
translationNotes.note: Both words mean timber or a stake, not a gallows with a rope; English versions supplied that later image. A cubit is about eighteen inches, so fifty cubits stands near seventy-five feet.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זֶרֶשׁ (Zeresh) - Greek: Ζωσάρα (Zosara)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew names her Zeresh. As with the eunuchs' names, the Greek carries a different spelling of the same Persian name, so the two books can look like they are naming different people.

stories.keyTakeaway: The king offers Esther half his kingdom, and she asks only that he and Haman come to her banquet. Over the wine he presses again, and she invites them back for a second banquet the next day. Haman leaves elated, rages at the sight of Mordecai in the courtyard, and on the advice of his wife Zosara has a pole fifty cubits high prepared.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 13
summaryBullets: That night the Lord took sleep from the king, so he told his servant to bring in the books, the daily records, and to read to him. (13:1).
He found the words written about Mordecai, how he had told the king about the two royal eunuchs who kept watch and sought to lay hands on Artaxerxes. (13:2).
The king said, “What honor or favor did we bestow on Mordecai?” The king’s servants said, “You have done nothing for him.” (13:3).

While the king was inquiring about the goodwill shown by Mordecai, Haman was there in the courtyard. The king asked, “Who is in the courtyard?” Now Haman had come in to speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on the pole he had prepared. (13:4).
The servants of the king said, “Look, Haman is standing in the courtyard.” And the king said, “Call him.” (13:5).
Then the king said to Haman, “What shall I do for the man whom I wish to honor?” And Haman said to himself, “Whom would the king wish to honor but me?” (13:6).
So he said to the king, “For the man whom the king wishes to honor, (13:7).
let the king’s servants bring out the fine linen robe that the king wears and the horse that the king rides, (13:8).

and let them be given to one of the king’s honored Friends, and let him robe the man whom the king loves and mount him on the horse and proclaim through the streets of the city, ‘Thus shall it be done for every man whom the king honors.’” (13:9).
Then the king said to Haman, “You have spoken well. Do just so for Mordecai the Jew, who attends in the court, and let not one word of what you have said be neglected.” (13:10).

So Haman got the robe and the horse. He put the robe on Mordecai and mounted him on the horse and went through the streets of the city, proclaiming, “Thus shall it be for every man whom the king wishes to honor.” (13:11).
Then Mordecai returned to the courtyard, but Haman returned home, mourning, with his head covered. (13:12).

Haman told his wife Zosara and his friends what had befallen him, and his friends and his wife said to him, “If Mordecai is of the Jewish people, and you have begun to be humbled before him, you will surely fall. You will not be able to defend yourself against him, for the living God is with him.” (13:13).
While they were still talking, the eunuchs arrived and hurried Haman away to the banquet that Esther had prepared. (13:14).
crossRefs: Esther 6:1-14: The Hebrew account of the sleepless night, the reading of the annals, and the honor given to Mordecai.
Daniel 6:18: A king passes the night sleepless, refusing food and every diversion.
Genesis 41:42-43: Pharaoh dresses Joseph in fine linen, sets him in the second chariot, and has a herald cry out before him.
1 Kings 1:33-34: The king's own mule given to the man he means to raise, with a proclamation through the city.
2 Samuel 15:30: David goes up the ascent of Olives weeping, with his head covered and his feet bare.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֵפֶר הַזִּכְרֹנוֹת דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים (sefer ha-zikhronot divrei ha-yamim) - Greek: γράμματα μνημόσυνα τῶν ἡμερῶν (grammata mnemosyna ton hemeron)
translationNotes.note: The Persian court kept a running daybook of business, petitions, and services rendered. It was read aloud to the king, which is why a report filed years earlier can surface intact in the middle of the night.

translationNotes.term: The robe the king wears and the horse the king rides
translationNotes.original: Greek: στολὴν βυσσίνην (stolen byssinen), fine linen robe
translationNotes.note: Wearing the king's own clothing or riding his horse put a man in the place of the king for as long as it lasted. This is why the request is so bold, and why the honor is worth more than money.

translationNotes.term: One of the king's honored Friends
translationNotes.original: Greek: τῶν φίλων τοῦ βασιλέως τῶν ἐνδόξων (ton philon tou basileos ton endoxon)
translationNotes.note: The Friends were the graded ranks of the court. Haman's proposal has one of the highest of them walking as a servant beside the horse, which is what makes the honor conspicuous.

translationNotes.original: Greek: λυπούμενος κατὰ κεφαλῆς (lypoumenos kata kephales)
translationNotes.note: Pulling a garment over the head was the recognized posture of grief and disgrace, done in public so it could be read at a glance. David goes up the Mount of Olives the same way.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Lord takes sleep from the king, who has the daily records read and finds Mordecai's unrewarded report of the two eunuchs. Haman, arrived to ask for Mordecai's hanging, is asked what should be done for the man the king honors, and names the royal robe and horse. The king orders it all done for Mordecai the Jew.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 14
summaryBullets: So the king and Haman went in to drink with the queen. (14:1).

And the second day, as they were drinking wine, the king said, “What is it, Queen Esther? What is your petition, and what is your request? It shall be granted to you, even to half of my kingdom.” (14:2).
She answered and said, “If I have found favor with the king, let my life be granted me at my petition and my people at my request. (14:3).

For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, plundered, and made slaves—we and our children—male and female slaves. I took no heed, but now our adversary brings shame on the king’s court.” (14:4).
Then the king said, “Who is the person who would dare to do this thing?” (14:5).
Esther said, “Our enemy is this evil man Haman!” At this, Haman was terrified in the presence of the king and queen. (14:6).
The king rose from the banquet and went into the garden, and Haman began to beg for his life from the queen, for he saw that he was in serious trouble. (14:7).

When the king returned from the garden, Haman had thrown himself on the couch, pleading with the queen. The king said, “Will you dare even assault my wife in my own house?” Haman, when he heard, turned away his face. (14:8).

Then Bugathan, one of the eunuchs, said to the king, “Look, Haman has even prepared a pole for Mordecai, who gave information of concern to the king; it is standing at Haman’s house, a pole fifty cubits high.” So the king said, “Let Haman be executed on that.” (14:9).
So Haman was hung on the pole that had been prepared for Mordecai. With that the anger of the king abated. (14:10).
crossRefs: Esther 7:1-10: The Hebrew account, which names the eunuch Harbona and ends with the king's wrath abating.
Deuteronomy 21:22-23: A body hung on a tree must not stay there overnight, for anyone so hung is under God's curse.
Amos 6:4-7: Those who lie on beds of ivory and lounge on their couches at their feasting.
Daniel 6:24: The men who accused Daniel are thrown into the den they had prepared for him.
Psalm 7:15-16: The one who digs a pit falls into it, and his violence comes down on his own head.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐπράθημεν (eprathemen)
translationNotes.note: The verb is the ordinary word for selling goods or persons. Esther puts the decree in the language of a transaction, which is exactly what it was: a people traded to the treasury for ten thousand talents.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐπὶ τὴν κλίνην (epi ten klinen)
translationNotes.note: Guests reclined on couches to eat rather than sitting at chairs. Haman is begging at the queen's feet, but because she is lying down, throwing himself on her couch puts him bodily over her, and the king reads it as assault.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ὁ διάβολος (ho diabolos)
translationNotes.note: The Greek word for a slanderer or accuser, someone who destroys another with words. The text uses it as Haman's standing description. It is the same word that later English Bibles render as the devil.

translationNotes.term: Let Haman be executed on that
translationNotes.original: Greek: σταυρωθήτω (staurotheto), and κρεμάννυμι (kremannymi), to hang
translationNotes.note: The first verb means to fasten to a stake or impale, the second to hang up. The Greek pictures a body fixed to a raised timber and left in view, which is what the fifty-cubit pole is for.

stories.keyTakeaway: At the second banquet the king again offers half his kingdom, and Esther asks for her life and her people's, saying they have been sold to destruction and slavery, and names Haman. The king storms into the garden; Haman falls on her couch to beg and is taken for assaulting the queen. Bugathan names the pole, and Haman is hung on it.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 15
summaryBullets: On that very day King Artaxerxes granted to Esther all that had belonged to Haman the accuser, and Mordecai was summoned by the king, for Esther had disclosed that he was related to her. (15:1).
The king took his signet ring, which he had taken back from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai; and Esther set Mordecai over everything that had been Haman’s. (15:2).
Then she spoke once again to the king and, falling at his feet, begged him to undo the harm done by Haman and all that he had done against the Jews. (15:3).
The king extended his golden scepter to Esther, and she rose and stood before the king. (15:4).
Esther said, “If it pleases you, and if I have found favor, let an order be written revoking the letters that Haman sent, which were written for the destruction of the Jews in your kingdom. (15:5).
How can I look on the ruin of my people, and how can I survive the destruction of my kindred?” (15:6).
The king said to Esther, “Now that I have granted you all that was Haman’s and have hanged him on the pole because he laid hands on the Jews, what more do you ask? (15:7).
Write in my name whatever you think best and seal it with my ring, for whatever is written at the king’s command and sealed with my ring cannot be contradicted.” (15:8).

The secretaries were summoned on the twenty-third day of the first month, which is Nisan, in the same year, and orders were written to the Jews, whatever the king had commanded to the local governors and rulers of the satrapies from India to Ethiopia, one hundred twenty-seven satrapies, province by province, each in its own language. (15:9).
The edict was written with the king’s authority and sealed with his ring, and they sent the letters by couriers. (15:10).
He ordered the Jews in every city to live by their own laws, to help one another, and to deal with their adversaries and those who attacked them as they pleased, (15:11).
on a single day, the thirteenth of the twelfth month, which is Adar, throughout all the kingdom of Artaxerxes. (15:12).
crossRefs: Esther 8:1-12: The Hebrew account of the same grant, the transfer of the ring, and the order to write a second decree.
Daniel 6:15: No decree or ordinance the king establishes may be changed under the law of the Medes and Persians.
1 Kings 21:15-16: The property of a condemned man is taken over as soon as sentence has been carried out.
Ezra 7:11-26: A Persian king's written commission to satraps and treasurers, granting a people the right to live by its own law.
Nehemiah 2:7-9: Sealed letters carried to the governors of a province, presented on arrival by the king's officers.

translationNotes.term: The twenty-third day of the first month, which is Nisan
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִיסָן (Nisan) - Greek: Νισα (Nisa)
translationNotes.note: Nisan is the first month of the Hebrew year, March into April. Haman's letters went out on the thirteenth of the same month, so this second writing follows the first by ten days.

translationNotes.term: Sealed with my ring cannot be contradicted
translationNotes.original: Greek: οὐκ ἔστιν αὐτοῖς ἀντειπεῖν (ouk estin autois anteipein)
translationNotes.note: Under Persian law a sealed royal order could not be cancelled, only answered by a further order. That is why the first decree is left standing and a second one written rather than the first withdrawn.

translationNotes.term: All that had belonged to Haman
translationNotes.original: Greek: ὅσα ὑπῆρχεν Αμαν (hosa hyperchen Aman)
translationNotes.note: The estate of a man condemned for treason fell to the crown. The king is not making a gift out of his own goods; he is regranting confiscated property, and with it the household and staff that came with it.

translationNotes.term: Province by province, each in its own language
translationNotes.original: Greek: κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν λέξιν (kata ten heauton lexin)
translationNotes.note: The Persian chancery issued orders in the languages of the provinces rather than in one imperial tongue, with Aramaic serving as the common administrative language across the empire.

stories.keyTakeaway: The king gives Esther all that was Haman's and gives Mordecai the signet ring taken back from him. Esther falls at the king's feet and begs that Haman's letters be revoked; he extends the golden scepter and tells her to write in his name and seal it with his ring. On the twenty-third of Nisan the orders go out to all one hundred twenty-seven satrapies.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 16
summaryBullets: This is a copy of the letter: “The Great King, Artaxerxes, to the governors of the one hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia and to those who are loyal to our government, greetings. (16:1).
Many people, the more they are honored with the generous kindness of their benefactors, the more arrogant do they become, (16:2).
and not only seek to injure our subjects but, unable to bear their own prosperity, they even scheme against their benefactors. (16:3).

They not only take away thankfulness from among men but, carried away by the boasts of those who know nothing of goodness, they suppose they will escape the justice of God, who hates evil and sees all things. (16:4).

And often many of those who are set in places of authority have been made partners in the shedding of innocent blood by the persuasion of friends entrusted with public affairs, and have been involved in irreparable calamities, (16:5).
when these persons, by the false trickery of an evil nature, have deceived the sincere goodwill of their rulers. (16:6).

What has been wickedly accomplished through the base conduct of those who hold power unworthily can be seen, not so much from the older records handed down to us, as from what lies close at hand if you examine it. (16:7).
In the future we will take care to render our kingdom quiet and peaceable for all, (16:8).
by changing our methods and always judging what comes before us with fair consideration. (16:9).
For Haman son of Hammedatha, a Macedonian, in truth an alien to the blood of the Persians and far removed from our kindness, was received as a guest among us (16:10).
and enjoyed so fully the goodwill we hold toward every nation that he was proclaimed our father and was bowed down to by all as the person second to the royal throne. (16:11).
But, unable to restrain his arrogance, he undertook to deprive us of our kingdom and our life, (16:12).

and with intricate craft and deceit he asked for the destruction of Mordecai, our deliverer and perpetual benefactor, and of Esther, the blameless partner of our kingdom, together with their whole nation. (16:13).
He thought that by these methods he would catch us undefended and transfer the rule of the Persians to the Macedonians. (16:14).
But we find that the Jews, whom this most wicked man consigned to destruction, are not evildoers but are governed by the most righteous laws (16:15).
and are children of the living God, most high and most mighty, who has directed the kingdom in the most excellent order for us and for our ancestors. (16:16).
You will therefore do well not to put into execution the letters sent by Haman son of Hammedatha, (16:17).
since the man who did these things has been hanged at the gate of Susa with all his household, God, who rules over all things, having swiftly repaid him as he deserved. (16:18).
Therefore post a copy of this letter publicly in every place, and permit the Jews to live under their own laws. (16:19).
And lend them support, so that on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, on that very day, they may defend themselves against those who attack them in a time of affliction. (16:20).
For God, who rules over all things, has made this day a day of gladness for his chosen people instead of a day of their destruction. (16:21).
Therefore you shall observe this as a notable day among your commemorative festivals, with all good cheer, (16:22).
so that both now and hereafter it may mean deliverance for us and for those loyal to the Persians, but for those who plot against us a reminder of destruction. (16:23).

Every city and country, without exception, that does not act accordingly shall be destroyed in wrath with spear and fire. It shall be made not only unapproachable to people but also most hateful to wild animals and birds forever.” (16:24).
crossRefs: Ezra 6:6-12: A Persian king orders his officials to support the Jews at royal expense and fixes a penalty for anyone who alters the decree.
Daniel 6:25-27: A Persian king writes to all peoples and languages, honoring the living God who rescues and delivers.
Luke 22:25: The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors.
Acts 15:23-29: A letter opening with greetings, sent out to be read in every place it concerns.
Isaiah 34:11-15: A land left desolate, handed over to wild creatures and birds forever.

translationNotes.original: Greek: χαίρειν (chairein)
translationNotes.note: The standard opening of a Greek official letter, following the names of sender and addressee. Its presence marks this document as a chancery letter in Greek form, the same formula used in the letter of Acts 15:23.

translationNotes.term: Haman son of Hammedatha, a Macedonian
translationNotes.original: Greek: Μακεδών (Makedon)
translationNotes.note: Earlier the same man is called a Bougean, and the Hebrew calls him an Agagite. Here the royal letter calls him a Macedonian and an alien to Persian blood, charging him with meaning to hand Persia to Macedon.

translationNotes.original: Greek: σωτὴρ καὶ εὐεργέτης (soter kai euergetes)
translationNotes.note: Two formal honors of the Hellenistic world, savior and benefactor, voted to kings and to men who had done the state a service. Ptolemy Euergetes carried the second as part of his royal name.

translationNotes.original: Greek: δόρατι καὶ πυρὶ (dorati kai pyri)
translationNotes.note: The penalty clause of the decree. Making a place unapproachable to people and hateful to beasts and birds is the standard curse of total desolation used in ancient treaties and royal orders.

stories.keyTakeaway: The second letter is quoted in full. Artaxerxes writes that men honored by their benefactors often turn arrogant, and that rulers are drawn into innocent blood by false counselors. He names Haman a Macedonian who schemed for the kingdom and reports him hanged with his household, orders his letters ignored, and commands that the Jews be supported and the day kept as a festival.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 17
summaryBullets: Let copies of the decree be posted conspicuously throughout the kingdom, and let all the Jews be ready on that day to fight against their enemies. (17:13).
So the messengers on horseback set out with all speed to carry out the king’s orders, and the decree was published also in Susa. (17:14).
Mordecai went out dressed in the royal robe and wearing a gold crown and a diadem of fine purple linen. When the people in Susa saw him, they rejoiced. (17:15).
And the Jews had light and gladness (17:16).

in every city and province wherever the decree was published, wherever the proclamation was posted, there was joy and gladness among the Jews, feasting and celebration. And many of the gentiles were circumcised and became Jews out of fear of the Jews. (17:17).
crossRefs: Esther 8:13-17: The Hebrew account of the posting, Mordecai's robes, and the gladness of the Jews in every province.
Exodus 12:48: A resident alien who wants to keep the Passover must first be circumcised, and then he is counted as native-born.
Psalm 97:11: Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart.
Daniel 5:29: A man is clothed in purple, given a gold chain, and proclaimed third in the kingdom.
Zechariah 8:23: Ten men from every language take hold of the robe of a Jew, saying they have heard that God is with you.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רָצִים (ratzim, runners) - Greek: ἱππεῖς (hippeis, horsemen)
translationNotes.note: The Persian empire ran a relay post of mounted riders with fresh horses staged along the royal roads. Nothing traveled faster in that world, and it was reserved for the king's business.

translationNotes.term: A gold crown and a diadem of fine purple linen
translationNotes.original: Greek: στέφανος χρυσοῦς καὶ διάδημα βύσσινον πορφυροῦν (stephanos chrysous kai diadema byssinon porphyroun)
translationNotes.note: Two separate things: the stephanos is a wreath or circlet, the diadema a band tied around the head. Purple dye came from sea snails at enormous cost, so the color itself announced rank.

translationNotes.original: Greek: φῶς καὶ εὐφροσύνη (phos kai euphrosyne)
translationNotes.note: A fixed pairing that means relief and public rejoicing rather than daylight. The words that follow it, joy and feasting, are the ordinary vocabulary of a festival kept in the streets.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִתְיַהֲדִים (mityahadim) - Greek: ιουδάιζον (ioudaizon)
translationNotes.note: The Greek verb ioudaizo means to live as a Jew, adopting the law and the customs. Paul uses the same verb in Galatians 2:14. Both texts describe joining the people, not merely favoring them.

stories.keyTakeaway: Copies of the decree go up throughout the kingdom, ordering the Jews to be ready on that day, and mounted couriers carry it at speed to Susa and beyond. Mordecai comes out in the royal robe, a gold crown, and a diadem of purple linen, and Susa rejoices. Wherever the decree is posted the Jews have light and gladness, and many gentiles become Jews.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 18
summaryBullets: Now on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is Adar, the letters written by the king arrived. (18:1).
On that same day the enemies of the Jews perished, for no one resisted, out of fear of them. (18:2).
The governors of the satrapies, the princes, and the royal secretaries were paying honor to the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai lay upon them. (18:3).
The king’s decree required that Mordecai’s name be held in honor throughout the kingdom. (18:4).
Now in the city of Susa the Jews killed five hundred men, (18:6).
including Pharsannestain, Delphon, Phasga, (18:7).
Pharadatha, Barea, Sarbacha, (18:8).
Marmasima, Aruphaeus, Arsaeus, and Zabutheus, (18:9).
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the Bougean, the enemy of the Jews; and they plundered their property on that same day. (18:10).
That same day the number of those killed in Susa was reported to the king. (18:11).

The king said to Esther, “In the city of Susa the Jews have killed five hundred men. What do you suppose they have done in the rest of the country? What more do you ask? It shall be done for you.” (18:12).
And Esther said to the king, “Let the Jews be allowed to do the same tomorrow, and let them hang the ten sons of Haman.” (18:13).
So he permitted this to be done and handed over to the Jews of the city the bodies of the sons of Haman to hang up. (18:14).
The Jews who were in Susa gathered on the fourteenth day of Adar and killed three hundred men, but they took no plunder. (18:15).

Now the other Jews in the kingdom gathered and helped one another and gained rest from their enemies, for they destroyed fifteen thousand of them on the thirteenth of Adar, but they took no plunder. (18:16).
On the fourteenth day of the same month they rested, and they kept it as a day of rest with joy and gladness. (18:17).
The Jews who were in the city of Susa gathered also on the fourteenth day and rested, and they kept the fifteenth as well with joy and gladness. (18:18).
On this account, then, the Jews who are scattered in every foreign land keep the fourteenth of Adar as a joyful holiday, sending portions of food to one another. (18:19).
Mordecai recorded these things in a book and sent it to the Jews in the kingdom of Artaxerxes, both those near and those far away, (18:20).
to institute these days as holidays and to keep the fourteenth and the fifteenth of Adar, (18:21).

for on these days the Jews got relief from their enemies, and in that month, which is Adar, their sorrow was turned into joy and their mourning into a holiday. They were to spend the whole month in good days of feasting and gladness, sending portions of food to their friends and to the poor. (18:22).
So the Jews accepted what Mordecai had written to them, (18:23).
how Haman son of Hammedatha, the Macedonian, fought against them, and how he made a decree and cast lots to destroy them utterly, (18:24).
and how he went in to the king to tell him to hang Mordecai; but the evils he had tried to bring upon the Jews came upon himself, and he was hanged, he and his children. (18:25).

Therefore these days were called Purim, because of the lots, for in their language they are called Purim, and because of the words of this letter, and because of all they had suffered on this account, and all that had happened to them. (18:26).

Mordecai established it, and the Jews took upon themselves, upon their descendants, and upon those who joined them, to observe it without fail. These days were to be a memorial kept in every generation, city, family, and province. (18:27).
These days of Purim shall be observed forever, and their memorial shall not fail in any generation. (18:28).
Then Queen Esther daughter of Aminadab, along with Mordecai the Jew, wrote down all that they had done, and the confirmation of the letter about Purim. (18:29).
And Mordecai and Queen Esther established this on their own responsibility, pledging at that time their own well-being to their plan. (18:31).
Esther established it by a decree forever, and it was written down as a memorial. (18:32).
crossRefs: Esther 9:1-32: The Hebrew account, which numbers the dead in the provinces at seventy-five thousand.
1 Samuel 15:17-23: Saul is condemned for keeping the spoil of the Amalekites after being told to leave it.
Nehemiah 8:10-12: A day kept with eating and drinking and portions sent to those who have nothing prepared.
Exodus 12:14: A day appointed as a memorial, kept as a festival throughout the generations as a lasting ordinance.
2 Samuel 21:12-14: The bodies of executed men are recovered from public display and given burial.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פּוּרִים (Purim), from פּוּר (pur, lot) - Greek: Φρουραι (Phrourai)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew names the festival from pur, the lot Haman cast. The Greek does not use that word; it writes the name as Phrourai and explains it as coming from the lots. English versions of the Greek print the familiar Purim.

translationNotes.original: Greek: μυρίους πεντακισχιλίους (myrious pentakischilious)
translationNotes.note: The Greek and Hebrew give different totals for the provincial dead. The Greek has fifteen thousand; the Hebrew has seventy-five thousand. The counts for Susa, five hundred and then three hundred, agree in both.

translationNotes.term: Hang the ten sons of Haman
translationNotes.original: Greek: τὰ σώματα τῶν υἱῶν Αμαν κρεμάσαι (ta somata ton huion Aman kremasai)
translationNotes.note: The Greek says bodies. The ten had already been killed the previous day; what is granted is the public display of the corpses on the timber, a recognized penalty added after death rather than a second execution.

translationNotes.original: Greek: οὐδὲν διήρπασαν (ouden dierpasan)
translationNotes.note: The decree allowed the taking of goods, as Haman's letters had allowed it against the Jews. The text records three separate times that they declined it, so the refusal is deliberate and not a lack of opportunity.

stories.keyTakeaway: On the thirteenth of Adar the letters arrive and the enemies of the Jews fall, no one resisting for fear of Mordecai. In Susa five hundred die with Haman's ten sons, three hundred more the next day, and fifteen thousand in the provinces, with no plunder taken. Mordecai writes to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar, called Purim after the lots.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 19
summaryBullets: The king levied a tax upon his kingdom both by land and by sea. (19:1).
And as for his power and bravery, and the wealth and glory of his kingdom, they are written in the book of the Persians and the Medes as a memorial. (19:2).
Mordecai succeeded King Artaxerxes and was great in the kingdom, honored by the Jews, and he lived his life beloved by his whole nation. (19:3).
crossRefs: Esther 10:1-3: The Hebrew account, which calls Mordecai second only to King Ahasuerus and great among the Jews.
