Genesis 41:40-44: A foreigner set over the whole land, second only to the throne, with all obeying his word.
Ezra 4:13: Tribute, custom, and toll withheld from a Persian king's revenue.
Nehemiah 5:4: People borrow money against their fields and vineyards to pay the king's tax.
1 Kings 14:19: The acts and the might of a king written in the Book of the Chronicles of his kingdom.

translationNotes.original: Greek: τέλη (tele)
translationNotes.note: Tele are dues and tolls rather than a single income tax. Persian revenue came as fixed tribute assessed on each satrapy in silver and in kind, with tolls added on roads, harbors, and river crossings.

translationNotes.term: Both by land and by sea
translationNotes.original: Greek: τῆς τε γῆς καὶ τῆς θαλάσσης (tes te ges kai tes thalasses)
translationNotes.note: The empire's assessment reached the coastal provinces and the islands as well as the inland satrapies, so the phrase describes the whole extent of what could be taxed, not two different taxes.

translationNotes.term: The book of the Persians and the Medes
translationNotes.original: Greek: βιβλίον βασιλέων Περσῶν καὶ Μήδων (biblion basileon Person kai Medon)
translationNotes.note: The royal chronicle, the same class of record read aloud to the sleepless king earlier in the book. Deeds entered there were preserved as a memorial, which is the standing claim of an official archive.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁנֶה לַמֶּלֶךְ (mishneh la-melekh, second to the king) - Greek: διεδέχετο (diedecheto)
translationNotes.note: The Greek verb means to come next in rank, to be the king's deputy. The Hebrew says plainly that Mordecai was second to the king. Neither text says he took the throne.

stories.keyTakeaway: The king levies a tax on his kingdom by land and by sea. His power and bravery and the wealth and glory of his kingdom are written in the book of the Persians and the Medes as a memorial. Mordecai comes next after King Artaxerxes, great in the kingdom, honored by the Jews, and loved by his whole nation.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 20
summaryBullets: And Mordecai said, “These things have come from God. (20:4).
For I remember the dream that I had concerning these matters, and not one detail of it has failed. (20:5).
There was the little spring that became a river, and there was light and the sun and abundant water. The river is Esther, whom the king married and made queen. (20:6).
The two dragons are Haman and myself. (20:7).
The nations are those that gathered to destroy the name of the Jews. (20:8).

And my nation, this is Israel, who cried out to God and were saved. The Lord saved his people; the Lord rescued us from all these evils. God did great signs and wonders such as have not happened among the nations. (20:9).
For this purpose he made two lots, one for the people of God and one for all the nations. (20:10).
And these two lots came to the hour and the time and the day of judgment before God and among all the nations. (20:11).
And God remembered his people and vindicated his inheritance. (20:12).

So they will observe these days in the month of Adar, on the fourteenth and the fifteenth of that month, with an assembly and joy and gladness before God, throughout the generations forever among his people Israel.” (20:13).
crossRefs: Genesis 41:25-32: A dream declared to be what God has determined to do, shown to the dreamer beforehand.
Daniel 2:28-30: God reveals what is to happen, and the interpretation is given so the king may know it.
Deuteronomy 25:19: The command to blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.
Deuteronomy 6:22: Signs and wonders done in Egypt before their eyes, recited as the reason for the ordinances.
Exodus 2:24: God hears the groaning of the people and remembers His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

translationNotes.original: Greek: κλήρους δύο (klerous dyo)
translationNotes.note: The same word used for the lots Haman cast to fix a day. The dream's interpretation puts the whole affair in that vocabulary, one lot against another, which is the link the festival's name preserves.

translationNotes.original: Greek: τὸ ὄνομα τῶν Ιουδαίων (to onoma ton Ioudaion)
translationNotes.note: To destroy a people's name is to end them so completely that nothing survives to be called by it, the same idea as blotting out a memory in Deuteronomy 25:19. It is stronger than killing a generation.

translationNotes.original: Greek: σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα (semeia kai terata)
translationNotes.note: A fixed pair used through the Greek Old Testament for the acts of God at the exodus. Using it here places what happened in Persia in the same class of event as what happened in Egypt.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐμνήσθη ὁ θεός (emnesthe ho theos)
translationNotes.note: In biblical usage remembering means acting on behalf of someone, not recovering a lost thought. The same verb covers God remembering Noah, the covenant with Abraham, and the groaning in Egypt.

stories.keyTakeaway: Mordecai says these things came from God and that not one detail of his dream failed. The little spring that became a river is Esther, the two dragons are Haman and himself, the nations are those who gathered to destroy the name of the Jews. God made two lots, one for His people and one for the nations, and both came to the day of judgment.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 21
summaryBullets: In the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, Dositheus, who said that he was a priest and a Levite, and his son Ptolemy brought the preceding letter about Purim, which they said was authentic and had been translated by Lysimachus son of Ptolemy, one of the residents of Jerusalem. (21:1).
crossRefs: Esther 9:29-32: The Hebrew records the letter about Purim written and sent out by Queen Esther and Mordecai with full authority.
Ezra 2:62: Men who claimed priestly descent but could not produce their family records were excluded from the priesthood.
Numbers 3:5-10: The Levites given to Aaron and his sons for the service of the sanctuary, with the priesthood kept to Aaron's line.
Nehemiah 8:8: The law read aloud and the sense given, so that the people understood the reading.
Jeremiah 51:59-64: A written scroll entrusted to a named man and carried to a distant city with instructions.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἡ προκειμένη ἐπιστολή (he prokeimene epistole), the preceding letter
translationNotes.note: A closing note recording who produced, translated, or delivered a book, written at the end of the scroll. Ancient books rarely carried title pages, so information of this kind belongs at the back.

translationNotes.term: The fourth year of Ptolemy and Cleopatra
translationNotes.original: Greek: ἔτους τετάρτου βασιλεύοντος Πτολεμαίου καὶ Κλεοπάτρας (etous tetartou basileuontos Ptolemaiou kai Kleopatras)
translationNotes.note: Dating by regnal year of a ruling pair was standard in Egypt. Several Ptolemies reigned alongside a Cleopatra, so the formula fixes a year within a reign without saying which royal pair is meant.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἱερεὺς καὶ Λευίτης (hiereus kai Leuites)
translationNotes.note: Two distinct standings. Every priest was a Levite, but only Aaron's line served as priests; the rest of the tribe assisted. The text says Dositheus claimed both, and reports it as his claim.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἑρμηνευκέναι (hermeneukenai)
translationNotes.note: The verb covers translating from one language into another and interpreting a difficult text. Naming the translator, his father, and his city is unusual; most ancient translations reached readers anonymously.

stories.keyTakeaway: In the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, Dositheus, who said that he was a priest and a Levite, and his son Ptolemy brought the preceding letter about Purim, which they said was authentic and had been translated by Lysimachus son of Ptolemy, one of the residents of Jerusalem.

intro:
This is the Greek text of Esther, the form in which the book stands in the Septuagint. It runs roughly a hundred verses longer than the Hebrew, and the surplus falls in six blocks that the Hebrew does not have: Mordecai's dream and his discovery of the plot against the king; the royal edict ordering the destruction of the Jews, quoted in full; the prayers of Mordecai and of Esther; Esther's approach to the throne uninvited; the counter-edict in favor of the Jews, also quoted in full; and Mordecai's interpretation of his dream, closing with a note on how the book reached Egypt. Modern editions letter the six A through F. In the Septuagint they stand inside the narrative rather than after it: A opens the book ahead of 1:1, B follows 3:13, C follows 4:17, D carries Esther into the king's presence where the Hebrew has 5:1-2, E follows 8:12, and F closes the book after 10:3.

The Greek names God outright where the Hebrew never does. Mordecai sees in his dream what God has determined to do (Addition A), and the two prayers address Him directly: Mordecai calls Him King of all powers and asks Him to spare His inheritance and turn the mourning into feasting, and Esther prays to the God of Abraham, confessing Israel's sin, saying she abhors the diadem she must wear in public, and asking for eloquence before the lion (Addition C). The Greek also differs from the Hebrew in names and dates. The king is Artaxerxes (Ἀρταξέρξης) throughout where the Hebrew has Ahasuerus (אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ); Haman is a Bougean where the Hebrew calls him an Agagite; and the lot falls on the fourteenth of Adar, where the Hebrew edict names the thirteenth (Esther 3:13). Addition F ends with a colophon recording how the book came to Egypt: in the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, Dositheus, who said he was a priest and a Levite, and his son Ptolemy brought the letter about Purim, which they said was authentic and had been translated by Lysimachus son of Ptolemy, a resident of Jerusalem. That names the translator, his city, and a regnal year, though not which royal pair is meant; the fourth year of a Ptolemy reigning with a Cleopatra falls either in 114 BC or in 78 BC. Josephus knew this fuller Greek form: retelling Esther in Antiquities of the Jews 11.184-296 (c. AD 93), he calls the king Artaxerxes, quotes both royal letters in full, and gives the prayers of Mordecai and Esther.

Jerome translated the Hebrew Esther for the Vulgate and then, rather than leave the Greek material where the Septuagint has it, gathered the six sections and set them after the end of the Hebrew book, marking each with an obelus and noting where in the story it belonged. Stephen Langton (died AD 1228), dividing the Latin Bible into chapters, numbered the appended material continuously with the rest, so Esther has sixteen chapters in the Vulgate against ten in the Hebrew, the six running as 10:4 through 16:24 in reverse narrative order, Mordecai's interpretation of the dream first and the dream itself last. Copyists frequently dropped Jerome's explanatory notes, which left the appendix reading as continuous text. The 1611 King James Bible carried the same appendix into its Apocrypha as "The rest of the Book of Esther." The English edition in this app follows the Greek arrangement instead, with the six sections standing where the Septuagint puts them, inside the story rather than piled at the end.

The Council of Hippo (AD 393) listed Esther among the canonical books and the Councils of Carthage (AD 397 and 419) repeated the list, the Latin Bible of that time carrying the book whole; the Council of Trent (session 4, AD 1546) received it entire. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles (AD 1571) lists "the rest of the Book of Esther" among the books the Church of England reads for example of life but not to establish doctrine, which is why English Bibles printing an Apocrypha carry that material separately. The Greek survives in two forms: the Septuagint text proper, carried by the great codices, and a shorter form preserved in a handful of minuscules and known as the Alpha text; both contain the six sections. The Greek title is Esther (Ἐσθήρ), from the Hebrew Ester (אֶסְתֵּר); the Hebrew book gives the same woman the name Hadassah (הֲדַסָּה), meaning "myrtle" (Esther 2:7). The events run at Susa, the Persian capital, under a king ruling one hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia, and the book accounts for the feast of Purim, named from the pur, the lot Haman cast to fix the day.
